endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Inform staff of how and where to report AI-related concerns during training, onboarding, and through supporting documentation such as AI fact sheets or model cards.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, ensure that personnel responsible for AI system monitoring and incident response activities are trained on procedures to share incident impacts with stakeholders.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: AI Actors should be aware of their roles in reporting AI incidents.

endorsements.title: The Clinicians' Guide to Large Language Models: A General Perspective With a Focus on Hallucinations
endorsements.quote: A crucial aspect in the deployment and judicious implementation of LLMs in a clinical setting lies in the establishment of a proactive error reporting program.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources endorse training staff to recognize, escalate, document, and report AI incidents, but no study has tested whether such training increases reporting or improves incident handling. The recommendation rests on expert consensus from governance frameworks and one commentary, and no supplied study documents how often AI incidents go unreported.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests AI incident training, and no supplied study measures the underreporting hazard it targets. The support comes from three frameworks and one commentary, which are expert opinion under GRADE conventions. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures reporting rates or response quality with and without training.

The endorsements are voluntary guidance. CHAI playbooks rate staff instruction on where to report as a must, while the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide and NIST AI 600-1 rate role training as a should. None of the supplied sources cites a statute or FDA or ONC rule that requires this training, so adoption depends on each health system's governance choices.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI incident reporting volume, time to escalation, documentation completeness, and patient harm before and after staff training, or across trained and untrained units. Studies should also establish how often AI incidents currently go unreported, and they should test which training formats and rules for sharing incident information staff retain in routine workflows.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot yet know whether staff training catches incidents that affect their patients, such as errors in translated or plain-language AI output, at the same rate as incidents affecting other patients.
